title: The Vote
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
We lost by one vote.

After months of hearings, petitions, neighborhood meetings, revised language, public arguments, private arguments, and one memorable session where Toph threatened to bend a councilman’s chair into a smaller chair, the Civic Balance Charter failed seven to six.

The chamber erupted.

Supporters shouted.

Opponents cheered.

Mara Sen said a word that caused three reporters to stop pretending not to listen.

I sat at the clerk’s table and stared at the tally.

Seven.

Six.

One vote.

The charter would have created enforceable anti-discrimination rules for city employment and housing, independent safety standards for bending and nonbending workers, public conflict-of-interest logs, and elected neighborhood councils with reserved nonbender representation where bending professions dominated local government.

It was not perfect.

That was part of why losing hurt.

We had compromised until every sentence had fingerprints on it.

The deciding vote belonged to Councilor Chen.

Of course it did.

He had spent six weeks describing himself as undecided and two days before the vote received a large campaign donation from an industrial association that opposed the worker-safety provisions.

Legal.

Technically.

I hated technically.

After the chamber emptied, a textile worker named Suri approached the clerk's table. Her hands were stained indigo, and she'd worn the same patched coat to every hearing. She had argued for the nonbender safety provisions so consistently that I recognized the scrape of her shoes on the tile before she spoke.

“I want a copy of the roll call,” she said.

“The votes are public,” the clerk answered.

“Not the speeches. The votes. I want my neighbors to know who actually stood up for the rule about fireproof exits.”

I pushed the tally sheet toward her. Her fingertip rested on Chen's name for a moment, then moved down the column.

“People will tell us we lost because we asked for too much,” she said. “I thought it wasn't too much to want to reach the door before a furnace explodes.”

“It isn't.”

“Then don't come back with a version where we have to give that up just to get six votes.”

I had been drafting concessions in my head since the result was called. The pages in my folder seemed to grow heavier.

“You might not like our next proposal,” I said.

“I might not. You're supposed to bring it to us before you ask me to sell it to the workshop.”

That hurt more than Chen's smug smile had. She was right. I'd started thinking of my neighbors as a constituency I needed to reassure instead of adults who could disagree with the strategy.

I wrote down her name and the workshop's requested meeting time, then stopped myself.

“May I give the committee your contact?”

“No. Tell them the union steward will send a representative. I've got a shift tomorrow.”

She took her copy of the votes and went. I sat with the ink drying under my hand, thinking of every time I'd told Aang he didn't get to decide the future for other people. Apparently the lesson was not reserved for the Avatar.

Aang stood in the public gallery.

He had refused to use Avatar authority to pressure the council.

That was correct.

I hated that too.

Katara sat beside him, jaw tight.

Toph was not allowed in the chamber after the chair incident.

She waited outside.

The council adjourned.

People poured into the hall.

Reporters surrounded Aang immediately.

“Avatar, will you override the vote?”

“Do you believe the council has failed nonbenders?”

“Will you withdraw support from Councilor Chen?”

Aang’s face went still in the public way.

“No,” he said. “The charter was a civil legislative process. I supported it publicly, but I will not turn disagreement into a reason for the Avatar to replace elected government.”

A reporter pushed closer. “Even when the result harms balance?”

Aang’s expression sharpened.

“Balance is not me getting every outcome I want.”

I heard the sentence.

I understood it.

I wanted to scream.

Mara caught my arm before I walked away.

“Don’t disappear.”

“I’m going outside.”

“You’re going home to write a better charter at two in the morning.”

“That is slander.”

“It’s prophecy.”

“I’m not the Avatar.”

“Thank every spirit available.”

I laughed despite myself.

Then I nearly cried.

Mara’s grip softened.

“Losing is part of politics.”

“I know.”

“There you go knowing things again.”

I glared.

She released me.

“Come to the meeting tomorrow.”

“What meeting?”

“The one where we decide what we do next.”

I stared at her.

“You scheduled it already?”

“I expected either victory problems or defeat problems.”

I loved her a little.

Outside, Toph leaned against the courthouse wall.

“Well?”

I did not need to answer.

She could hear the crowd.

“Seven-six,” I said.

Toph’s mouth flattened.

“Chen?”

“Yes.”

“Chair.”

“No.”

“Tiny chair.”

“No.”

“Stool?”

“Toph.”

She kicked the wall.

A small crack appeared.

“Property damage,” I said automatically.

“Put it on my tab.”

Katara emerged next.

She looked furious enough to freeze the rain.

Aang followed, surrounded by aides.

One handed him another schedule.

Aang looked at it.

Then tore it in half.

Everyone stopped.

The aide stared.

Aang said, “I’m going home.”

It was a tiny rebellion.

I loved it.

At home, nobody spoke for the first ten minutes.

Toph opened the bottle she had bought for the housing hearing months ago.

Katara made tea because she said we were not drinking on empty stomachs.

Aang sat on the kitchen floor with his back against a cabinet.

I put the vote tally on the table.

Seven.

Six.

Toph tapped the paper.

“So we change one.”

Katara sat across from me. “Or the language.”

Aang rubbed both hands over his face.

“Or the public.”

I looked at him.

He lowered his hands.

“Chen can take money because voters don’t punish him for it.”

“That’s cynical,” Katara said.

“It’s also true,” I said.

Aang sighed.

“I’m trying to be less naive.”

Toph pointed at him. “Don’t overcorrect. You’ll get boring.”

He threw a towel at her.

She caught it.

I stared at the tally.

“I thought if the argument was good enough…”

Mara’s voice echoed in my head.

Losing is part of politics.

Katara said, “Arguments matter. So does power.”

Aang looked at her.

She continued. “Who has money. Who has time to attend meetings. Who gets believed. Who is afraid of losing work if they sign a petition.”

Toph added, “Who owns the building the meeting happens in.”

I looked at her.

“That was almost profound.”

“Shut up.”

We spent the evening not solving it.

That was harder than solving things.

Aang kept reaching for possibilities and putting them back down because each one crossed some line of influence he did not want to cross.

Katara wanted accountability immediately and hated that due process was slow.

Toph wanted direct pressure and hated any system that rewarded politeness from people with less power.

I wanted to rewrite the text until language could defeat money.

None of us got what we wanted.

Around midnight, I stood to get my folders.

Three voices said, “No.”

I stopped.

“This is different.”

Toph threw the towel again.

“It’s midnight, Paperwork.”

“We just lost.”

“Yeah,” Katara said. “We lost.”

She came around the table.

“And you are not going to turn losing into punishment.”

I looked at her.

Aang’s expression softened.

“No penance by paperwork.”

“That phrase is offensive.”

“It’s good,” Toph said.

“Betrayal.”

Katara took my hand.

“Go to bed.”

I did.

Badly.

At three in the morning, I woke and found Aang sitting by the window.

“So much for rest,” I whispered.

He smiled faintly.

“I was trying.”

I sat beside him.

The city outside was dark except for factory lamps and a few late windows.

“Do you regret not intervening?” I asked.

Aang took a long time to answer.

“Yes.”

That surprised me.

“And no.”

“Very helpful.”

“I could have pressured Chen.”

“Yes.”

“People would probably praise me for it.”

“Yes.”

“And then the next Avatar might pressure a council for something worse.”

I leaned my head against the wall.

“Duty is annoying.”

Aang laughed quietly.

“I thought you liked rules.”

“I like rules other people follow.”

Toph’s voice came from the hallway.

“I heard that.”

We both jumped.

She walked in carrying a blanket.

Katara followed with three more.

“You’re all terrible at sleeping,” she said.

“We were having a constitutional discussion,” Aang said.

“At three in the morning.”

“Democracy never rests.”

Toph groaned. “Kill it.”

Katara draped a blanket over all of us.

We sat by the window until dawn.

We had lost.

No hidden victory.

No miraculous reversal.

Just one vote and the work after it.

When sunlight reached the factory roofs, I finally understood why the defeat mattered to the story we were building.

Love did not guarantee justice.

Good arguments did not guarantee votes.

Power used carefully was still power.

Duty sometimes meant refusing the shortcut even when the shortcut led somewhere you desperately wanted to go.

At nine, I went to Mara’s meeting.

I left my pen at home on purpose.

Toph brought me another one.

Mara’s meeting took place in a bakery after closing.

Nobody had reserved a hall. Nobody had an agenda printed on official paper. Someone wrote discussion points on the back of flour invoices and passed them around with leftover rolls.

I listened.

That was harder than speaking.

A machinist wanted the charter split into smaller ordinances so opponents could not kill every reform with one vote. A teacher argued that doing so would let the council approve symbolic pieces while avoiding the parts that redistributed actual authority. Two shop owners disagreed about whether another public hearing would help or merely repeat the same speeches.

No one asked me to solve it.

Eventually Mara looked over. “You’ve been quiet.”

“I’m practicing.”

“Painful?”

“Excruciating.”

The room laughed.

I unfolded my hands. “The council knows how to defeat our current proposal. So we stop giving them the same proposal.”

That started another hour of argument.

Good.

When I came home, Toph was asleep on the couch with a pen tucked behind one ear. Aang had fallen asleep on the floor beside a stack of cultural-school applications. Katara was still awake, reading by the stove.

“How was it?” she asked.

“Messy.”

Her smile said she understood.

I sat beside her.

“We might lose again.”

“Yes.”

“That doesn’t make tonight pointless?”

“No.”

I leaned my head against her shoulder.

Across the room, Toph muttered without opening her eyes, “Told you.”

“You were asleep.”

“Still right.”

The first vote had taught me something ugly and useful: losing did not automatically mean the work had failed. Sometimes it meant the strategy had.

The next morning, my borrowed pen was still on the table. I returned it to Toph.

She pushed it back.

“Keep it.”

“For luck?”

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

I kept it anyway.

I used that pen at the next meeting. We still argued. This time, losing was no longer the only ending I could imagine.
